newsitem.title: UK: Former minister asks Japan for POW compensation.
newsitem.headline: Former minister asks Japan for POW compensation.

text.p: Former British foreign secretary Douglas Hurd on Wednesday called on Japan to provide more compensation for people held in Japanese prison camps during World War Two.

Backed by parliamentarians from other parties and watched from the public galleries by survivors of the camps, Hurd said the Japanese government had not gone far enough to compensate for the pain and suffering of the prisoners of war.
But Foreign Office minister Jeremy Hanley told Hurd Britain's hands were tied by the 1951 San Francisco peace treaty which set compensation for the camp inmates.
Hurd told parliament he had been advised of the limits set by the 1951 treaty when he was minister.

But he told the House of Commons: "I know the difficulties of finding a way. But as a strong friend and supporter of modern Japan, I believe the search...for a way for more substantial action needs to continue."
Around 50,000 British men and women, soldiers and civilians, were held in Japanese camps and many died, Labour MP Dennis McShane told parliament. Some 10,000 were still alive.
Hanley said the government would continue discussions with Japan. Hurd's successor as foreign secretary, Malcolm Rifkind, raised the issue of former prisoners during a visit to Tokyo in August.
